claims.claim: Medicare and Medicaid were created in 1965 as Titles XVIII and XIX of the Social Security Act; Medicare is federal while Medicaid was an expanded federal-state medical-assistance program.

Medicare primarily covers people age 65 and older, plus certain younger people with long-term disabilities and people with end-stage renal disease, and its rules are set federally and apply nationwide.

Medicare Part A covers inpatient hospital, skilled nursing facility, hospice, and some home health care; Part B covers outpatient/physician services; Part C (Medicare Advantage) delivers Parts A and B through private Medicare-contracted plans; Part D covers prescription drugs.

Medicare is financed through two federal trust funds: the Hospital Insurance (HI) trust fund pays for Part A and is funded mainly by payroll taxes; the Supplementary Medical Insurance (SMI) trust fund pays for Parts B and D and is funded largely by congressionally authorized general revenue plus enrollee premiums.
The Medicare (HI) payroll tax is 1.45 percent on employees and 1.45 percent on employers (2.9 percent total) with no wage cap, plus an additional 0.9 percent on wages above $200,000.

Medicaid is a joint federal-state, means-tested program in which the federal government sets broad rules and shares cost while states run their own programs and set many eligibility and benefit rules within federal limits, so eligibility varies by state.
The federal share of Medicaid is set by the FMAP formula, which pays a higher share to lower-income states, with a statutory minimum of 50 percent and maximum of 83 percent.

The ACA created a new adult eligibility group covering adults under 65 with incomes up to an effective 138 percent of the federal poverty level (statutory 133 percent plus a 5 percent income disregard), with the federal government paying 90 percent of the cost for the expansion group.

In NFIB v. Sebelius (decided June 28, 2012) the Supreme Court effectively made the ACA Medicaid expansion optional for states by barring the withdrawal of existing Medicaid funds from states that decline to expand.
As of April 2025, 41 states and the District of Columbia had adopted the ACA Medicaid expansion.
About 32.8 million people were enrolled in Medicare Advantage (Part C) in 2024, roughly 54 percent of eligible Medicare beneficiaries.

About 12 million people were dually eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid in 2023 (roughly 9 million full-benefit and 3 million partial-benefit), and for them Medicare is generally the primary payer while Medicaid covers cost-sharing and services Medicare excludes such as long-term care.
Both Medicare and Medicaid (and CHIP) are administered and overseen at the federal level by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) within HHS.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Total current Medicaid/CHIP enrollment differs by source and reporting month.
positions: KFF enrollment tracker reported about 73.9 million enrolled in Medicaid/CHIP nationally as of April 2026, drawing on CMS administrative data.
CMS/Medicaid.gov monthly highlights reported roughly 75.7 million (October 2025) and 75.7 million-range point-in-time counts in late 2025.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson does not hinge on a single national enrollment total, so no specific Medicaid/CHIP grand-total figure was asserted in the prose; the two sources are consistent to within normal month-to-month and measurement variation. Where a total is discussed conceptually, it is framed as 'well over 140 million' combined across both programs, which both program figures comfortably support.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The ACA statute specifies 133 percent FPL, but eligibility is commonly cited as 138 percent FPL.
positions: Statutory text: 133 percent of the federal poverty level.
Effective level: 138 percent, because of a mandatory 5 percentage-point income disregard.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the effective 138 percent figure and explains it equals the statutory 133 percent plus the 5 percent disregard, so both are represented accurately.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('a foundational concept in Health Administration') and made no substantive, checkable claims about Medicare or Medicaid.
